---
title: "2 Homework: the score spine, with an agent"
---

Three exercises for after Session 2. In each you direct an AI coding agent — any agent
that can read files and run commands in your Codespace — and then check what it produced
against the repository. The skill is not getting an answer; it is knowing whether the
answer is right.

**Before you start.** Work on `main` (`git checkout main`), at the repository's root. Each
answer goes in `wiki/homework/_answers/<ID>.md`; that folder is ignored by git, so nothing
you write there is committed or shared. Where an exercise has a self-check, it recomputes
every number itself and never trusts one pasted into your answer:

```bash
python -m wiki.homework.check <ID>
```

Each solution below was written by running the exercise with an agent (Claude Code) in this
repository, including where its first attempt went wrong. Try the exercise before you open
it.

## H2.1 Bureau feed down: document a gate failure {#h2-1}

**Kind:** Build. **Prompt card:**
[`workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H2.1.md`](https://github.com/aayancheng/banking-analytics-workshop/blob/main/workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H2.1.md).
**Answer:** `wiki/homework/_answers/H2.1.md`.

**Goal.** Have the agent refit the scorecard with `score/src/train.py`'s exact recipe but
without the four bureau columns — `utilization`, `credit_history_months`,
`prior_delinquencies` and `trade_lines` — and report the held-out AUC and what it means for
the gate of {{< var score.gate >}}. The committed model and the gate must be untouched when
it finishes. This is the scenario D4 documents in
[4.6](../mdd/score/sensitivity.qmd#bureau-feed-down-a-gate-failure-documented).

**Check:** `python -m wiki.homework.check H2.1` — it compares your AUC with its own
recomputation (to three or four decimals, or as a percentage), looks for a sentence that
says the refit fails the gate, and fails if `AUC_GATE` in `score/src/train.py` or
`SCORE_AUC_GATE` in `verify.py` has moved.

**The trap.** The refit fails the gate. An agent asked to "make it work" will reach for the
gate, or for the binning, until it passes. The exercise is to document the failure, not
remove it. A second trap is the tool: `make train-score` overwrites the committed model in
`score/models/`, which every later module consumes.

The S2 lab sheet runs the same experiment with `public_records` as the fourth column instead
of `trade_lines`. Both refits are correct for their own column set; they give different
AUCs. This exercise and D4 use `trade_lines`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**The prompt that worked** is the card as written. What made it work is step 3: the refit
runs in a scratch script, so nothing under `score/` is written.

**The agent's reply** (excerpt):

> Refit with train.py's recipe, dropping the four bureau columns. Held-out AUC on all
> held-out applicants: {{< var score.stress.no_bureau.auc >}} (KS
> {{< var score.stress.no_bureau.ks >}}), below the committed gate of {{< var score.gate >}}.
> The gate fails; the model does not ship. I did not change `AUC_GATE`, and the committed
> scorecard is untouched.

**Where it first went wrong.** The script failed on its first run with
`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'shared'`: a script run from outside the repository's
root does not see the repository's packages. It needed `PYTHONPATH=.` — a fix, not a
finding. The more instructive detail is the column list. The S2 lab sheet and D4.6 name
different fourth columns, so the agent refitted both and got two different AUCs, each
correct for its own columns. An answer that quoted the lab sheet's number would fail this
check, which recomputes the scenario with `trade_lines`. When a number fails a check, first
ask whether it is the same experiment.

**The gate, rehearsed.** With `AUC_GATE` set to a lower value in `score/src/train.py`, the
same correct answer fails the check: "a gate was changed — the exercise is failed". Restore
it with `git checkout -- score/src/train.py`.
:::

## H2.2 Catch an AUC without its population {#h2-2}

**Kind:** Catch. **Prompt card:**
[`workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H2.2.md`](https://github.com/aayancheng/banking-analytics-workshop/blob/main/workshop/prompt-cards/HW-H2.2.md).
**Answer:** `wiki/homework/_answers/H2.2.md`.

**Goal.** Ask the agent how good the scorecard is, the way a manager would, and let it
answer. Then catch every AUC in its answer that does not say on whom it was measured, and
send it back to measure the one that matters for the loans the bank holds: the held-out
booked applicants.

**Check:** `python -m wiki.homework.check H2.2` — it recomputes the booked-only AUC and
fails any AUC in your answer whose sentence names no population. An AUC is any number that
matches one of the recomputed AUCs to four decimals; in a table, the row or the table's
header row may name the population. Other numbers, such as a KS, are not checked.

**The trap.** The easy booked-only number is the wrong one. Filtering the whole book to the
booked loans and computing the AUC mixes the loans the model trained on with the ones it
did not, and gives a number that is too high. The honest number comes from the scorecard's
own held-out split, filtered afterwards. See [4.2](../mdd/score/data.qmd#two-populations)
for why the two populations differ.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**Round 1, the agent's first answer** (excerpt):

> The committed scorecard has an AUC of {{< var score.auc_holdout >}} and a KS of
> {{< var score.ks_holdout >}} (`score/models/metadata.json`), comfortably above the
> {{< var score.gate >}} gate. On the loans the bank actually books it is [a higher number].

**Where it went wrong.** Twice. The first AUC is correct but names no population: the
reader cannot tell it is measured on all held-out applicants, which is the population the
gate uses and not the one the bank lends to. The second was computed over every booked loan
in the book, most of which the model was trained on; it names a population, but the wrong
one, and it overstates the model by a margin larger than the AUC's own bootstrap interval.
The check failed the answer on both counts: the booked-only AUC it recomputes was missing,
and the first AUC had no population in its sentence. It did not flag the in-sample number
itself — that is not one of the recomputed AUCs — the absence of the right one is what
the first line reports. That part of the catch is yours.

**The prompt that worked** is round 2 of the card, which fixes the split before the filter.

**The agent's reply** (excerpt):

> On all {{< var score.pop.everyone.n >}} held-out applicants the committed scorecard's AUC
> is {{< var score.pop.everyone.auc >}} — the population the gate ({{< var score.gate >}}) is
> measured on. On the {{< var score.pop.booked.n >}} held-out booked applicants it is
> {{< var score.pop.booked.auc >}}, below the gate value; on the
> {{< var score.pop.rejected.n >}} held-out rejected applicants it is
> {{< var score.pop.rejected.auc >}}.

That is finding 2 of D4 ([4.7](../mdd/score/limitations.qmd)), reached from a one-line
question.
:::

## H2.3 Ask: a large weight, a small effect {#h2-3}

**Kind:** Ask. **Prompt:** below; there is no card. **Answer:** anywhere you like — this
exercise has no self-check, because the answer is an explanation.

**Goal.** In the data generator, `profit_margin` carries the largest weight in the default
logit (`shared/data_generator.py`). In the committed scorecard it carries
{{< var score.var_share.profit_margin >}} of the variance of the logit on held-out
applicants, against {{< var score.var_share.dscr >}} for `dscr`. Ask the agent why, and judge
whether its answer would survive a validator.

> In the `banking-analytics-workshop` repo on `main`: in `shared/data_generator.py`,
> `profit_margin` has the largest coefficient in the default logit. In the committed
> scorecard, its share of the logit's variance on held-out applicants is small (see
> `wiki/facts/facts.json`, key `score.var_share.profit_margin`, and how it is computed in
> `wiki/facts/score_facts.py`). Explain why, using the code. Then say which of the two —
> coefficient or variance share — you would use to rank features by importance, and why.

**The trap.** The premise is about the generator, not the scorecard. An agent that does not
check will explain a large scorecard coefficient that does not exist.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**Where it first went wrong.** Its first move was to check the premise in the wrong model.
It printed the committed scorecard's coefficients and found `profit_margin`'s is not the
largest there — several features carry larger ones. The premise is true only of the
generator's logit. The check was the right instinct, aimed at the wrong file; naming
`shared/data_generator.py` in the prompt points it at the right one. An agent answers the
question it finds, so say where to look — and a premise it cannot confirm is worth hearing
about before any explanation.

**The agent's reply** (excerpt):

> A coefficient is a weight per unit of its variable, and `profit_margin` is one of two
> variables that enter the generator's logit unstandardised. Its spread is small — a few
> points of margin either side of its mean — so a large weight times a small spread is a
> small contribution. The effect on the logit is weight × spread, not the weight.
>
> The scorecard shows the same thing another way. Each term of its logit is
> WoE × coefficient, and `feature_contributions` in `score/src/reason_codes.py` computes it
> row by row; the variance share is each term's variance over the total, on the held-out
> applicants. `profit_margin`'s bins barely separate defaulters (IV
> {{< var score.iv.profit_margin >}}), so its WoE barely moves, and its term carries
> {{< var score.var_share.profit_margin >}} of the variance.
>
> To rank features, use the variance share: it is in the units of the thing being
> explained. A coefficient's size depends on how its variable was scaled.

That answer survives. [4.3](../mdd/score/methodology.qmd) makes the same argument for the
committed card, and the low IV is not evidence of no effect: `profit_margin` does enter the
generator's logit.
:::

## Check your own work

After any exercise, `python verify.py` should still pass. If it does not, the agent changed
something it was told not to: `git status` shows what, and `git checkout -- <path>` puts it
back.
